extracted.intended_audience: artists, aestheticians, critics, and educated readers interested in art theory (late‑19th century/modernist debate)
extracted.subtask_description: Normative guidance for evaluating and producing art: argues art's aim is moral transmission of the highest feelings, critiques aesthetic theories that equate beauty with goodness or celebrate obscurity and elite exclusiveness, and lays out practical standards (intelligibility, subject‑matter, accessibility, sincerity).

rubrics_metrics.name: Aim of art: transmission of the highest and best feelings
rubrics_metrics.description: Art is a human activity whose purpose is to transmit to others the highest and best feelings to which men have risen, rather than merely to afford refined pleasure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tolstoy contrasts true art (which communicates profound, elevating feelings) with art that exists to furnish pleasure to a narrow class. Example: prophets and universal artists transmitted religiously rooted feelings; by contrast, contemporary upper‑class art aims at enjoyment. Use this as primary test: does a work successfully communicate sincere high feeling to others?

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral purpose: art should serve goodness, not merely beauty
rubrics_metrics.description: Art should be judged by whether it serves goodness (moral ends), not by whether it is ‘beautiful’ in an æsthetic sense; beauty is not identical with goodness and often contrasts with it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rejects Baumgartenian/modern æsthetic doctrine that equates Beauty, Truth, and Goodness as a trinity. Historical note: Greeks tended to conflate beauty and good because of a lower moral ideal; Tolstoy insists Christian/Jewish perception recognizes moral goodness distinct from beauty. Evaluate works for their moral influence rather than only formal beauty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Universality and accessibility: art must be accessible to all people
rubrics_metrics.description: If art is truly important and spiritual (like religion), it should be accessible to everybody; art that is available only to an elite is not the art of all humanity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accessibility has two dimensions: intelligibility (understanding) and practical access (cost, distribution). Tolstoy argues the upper‑class art excludes 99% of people both economically and culturally; the defenders' argument that society might change to give access is criticized as implausible. As a criterion: prefer works that can be understood and experienced by broad audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intelligibility/clarity: art should aim to be intelligible to common people
rubrics_metrics.description: A universal artist composes so that his production is intelligible to all men; deliberately obscure, cryptic, or puzzle‑making art that privileges the initiated is a vice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tolstoy singles out Symbolists/Decadents (Baudelaire, Verlaine, Mallarmé and later followers) for elevating obscurity into a dogma—techniques like euphemism, mythological/historical allusion, deliberate vagueness and 'the enigma' are criticized. Use as negative test: art that requires initiation or special preparation to 'enjoy' fails the universality criterion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subject‑matter freshness: art must transmit new feelings, not recycle mere enjoyment
rubrics_metrics.description: A genuine work of art brings a new feeling into human life; mere repetition of previously known pleasures (enjoyment) is not real art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tolstoy analogizes to thought: only new thought is real. He emphasizes children's strong reaction to truly new feelings. Practical implication: evaluate whether a work conveys feelings that feel novel or deepen human feeling, rather than appealing primarily to habitual pleasurable sensations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Source of fresh feelings: religious perception as generator of authentic emotion
rubrics_metrics.description: Religious perception (the moral/spiritual understanding expressed in religions) is the source of endless, fresh feelings for art; art grounded in religious perception yields richer, more varied emotions than art grounded in the pursuit of enjoyment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical examples: Homer and Greek tragedy (from Greek religious perception), the prophets (Jewish perception), medieval Christian art (Catholic communal feeling). Tolstoy argues that art divorced from religious perception impoverishes subject‑matter; when assessing sources for subject‑matter, prize works tied to deep moral/religious perception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sincerity and naturalness: avoid artificial, affected, 'brain‑spun' art
rubrics_metrics.description: Art should be natural and sincere; art produced for a small, exceptional circle tends to become affected, obscure, and 'brain‑spun' rather than genuine and heartfelt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tolstoy links exclusivity and craftiness (allusions, euphemisms) to loss of sincerity. As an evaluative rule, prize spontaneous, direct expression of feeling and treat overly contrived or self‑conscious mannerisms as defects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject elitist exclusivity: art should not be produced solely for elite enjoyment
rubrics_metrics.description: Art made intentionally for an elite (‘the elect’, 'schöne Geister', 'Übermenschen') that excludes the mass of humanity is not the universal art and contributes to social corruption.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tolstoy documents how upper‑class art both depends on and perpetuates the slavery/poverty of masses; some defenders admit and embrace the exclusivity (open elitism). Critically assess whether a work's purpose, distribution, or form presupposes or relies on elite exclusiveness; if so, mark it as failing the universal art standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejecting the æsthetic trinity as an evaluative foundation
rubrics_metrics.description: The fashionable doctrine that treats Beauty, Truth, and Goodness as a single æsthetic trinity (and builds a science of æsthetics that treats beauty as the primary aim) is ideologically driven and unfounded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tolstoy argues Baumgarten’s æsthetics is an eighteenth‑century invention that served the tastes of upper classes and was later repeated uncritically. Use this as methodological guidance: do not let abstract axioms about 'beauty' displace concrete moral and communicative criteria when evaluating art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid narrow, trivial subject focus (pride, sexual desire, weariness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Upper‑class contemporary art is denounced for being overwhelmingly concentrated on a few trivial feelings—pride, sexual desire, and weariness of life—which produces impoverished subject‑matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tolstoy gives many examples (novels, songs, paintings emphasizing nakedness and eroticism, adultery themes, salon love affairs). When judging modern works, question whether they merely recycle these limited themes; favor works engaging broader, deeper human conditions (labor, communal life, religious feeling).
